<explanation>
Below is a detailed explanation and set of instructions for creating a system design diagram that accurately reflects the architecture of Defuddle. Based on the file structure and README, Defuddle is a JavaScript/TypeScript library that extracts main content from web pages by “defuddling” them, which involves removing clutter such as navigation, comments, and banners. It is built to work both in browser environments and on the server (with JSDOM). It also comes in two bundles—a core (lightweight) version and a full (feature-rich) version that adds advanced math conversion capabilities using libraries like mathml-to-latex and temml.

Below are the key aspects to capture in your system design diagram:

1. Main Components:
   • Defuddle Engine – The heart of this library. It includes the core parsing functionality that takes in a DOM document and outputs an article object having properties like content, title, metadata, math content, and more.
   • Elements Modules – Under the src/elements directory, you have several modules that handle specific parts of content standardization:
     - Code: Handles formatting and standardization of code blocks.
     - Headings: Manages the extraction and transformation of heading elements.
     - Math Modules: (math.base.ts, math.core.ts, math.full.ts, math.ts) These modules deal with converting math content including MathML elements. The “full” bundle uses the advanced math libraries.
   • Metadata Extraction & Constants – These modules (metadata.ts, constants.ts) deal with gathering page meta-data and defining important constants.
   • Types & Interfaces – The types.ts file defines the contract for the article object and supports type safety across the system.
   • Bundles – Two entry points are provided: one in src/index.ts for the core bundle and one in src/index.full.ts for the full bundle that integrates additional math conversion capabilities.

2. Relationships and Interactions between Components:
   • The consumer calls the Defuddle constructor (from src/defuddle.ts) with a DOM document (and optional settings such as debug) and then invokes the parse() method.
   • The parse method orchestrates the process by calling several helper modules/functions:
      - It delegates heading and code block standardization to the corresponding element modules.
      - For math content, depending on whether the core or full bundle is used, different math conversion modules are invoked.
      - Metadata extraction is integrated to produce the final article output.
   • External integrations:
      - In server-side usage, an external package (e.g., JSDOM) is used to create a DOM, which then is passed to Defuddle.
      - In the full bundle, external libraries such as mathml-to-latex and temml are integrated.
      
3. Architectural Patterns and Design Principles:
   • Modularity – The clear separation into different modules (elements, metadata, constants, types) supports a modular, loosely-coupled architecture.
   • Extensibility – The design anticipates future extensions (e.g., new element modules, additional metadata extraction, alternative math conversion).
   • Bundle Variants – Separation between the “core” and “full” functionality shows the use of feature toggles/build-time decisions in the architecture.
   • Configurability – Options such as debug mode indicate that the system is designed to run in various environments with customizable behavior.

4. Relevant Technologies/Frameworks:
   • TypeScript – The entire project is written in TypeScript, and you should denote that in your diagram.
   • Webpack – Indicate that Webpack is used for bundling.
   • External libraries: 
      - For advanced math conversion in the full bundle (e.g., mathml-to-latex, temml).
      - JSDOM for server-side HTML parsing.
  
5. Guidelines for the Diagram’s Tailoring:
   • Since Defuddle is a library rather than a full-stack application, focus on detailing the internal modules and the call sequence within the parsing method.
   • Emphasize the processing stages: Input DOM (from browser or JSDOM) → Defuddle Engine → Element-specific processors (for headings, code blocks, math, and footnotes) → Metadata extraction → Output article object.
   • Use two distinct paths or branch labeling to show the divergence between the core and full bundle (especially prominent with the math processing element).

6. Inclusion of Visual Elements:
   • Components: Represent each module (Defuddle Engine, individual element modules, metadata extraction, types, constants) as separate boxes with clear labels.
   • Data Flow Arrows: Draw directional arrows to indicate:
      - Input (DOM document) entering through the Defuddle constructor.
      - Flow from the Defuddle Engine to each element module and back.
      - The merging of module outputs into the final article object.
      - External dependencies (JSDOM on the server; math libraries in the full bundle) with arrows indicating their influence.
   • Color Coding/Shapes: For instance:
      - Use one shape/color to represent core processing modules.
      - Use special markers or another color for external integrations (like JSDOM and full-bundle specific math libraries).
      - Differentiate between configuration/metadata modules and content processing modules.

7. Detailed Diagram Elements to Include:
   • Label the Defuddle constructor and parse() method as central processing logic.
   • Highlight the “Elements” sub-system: Show how the individual modules (code, headings, various math modules) feed into the processing pipeline.
   • Show the integration of configuration files (like tsconfig and webpack.config.js) as peripheral artifacts that impact the build and module bundling.
   • Optionally sketch the build flow from source (src) to the distributable (dist/index.js) to represent deployment/or bundling, if relevant.

Following this explanation and these detailed instructions will ensure the system design diagram is comprehensive and reflects the modular, configurable, and extensible architecture of Defuddle. This diagram will thus serve as an effective tool for understanding the internal workings of the content extraction pipeline and its external integrations, making it easier to reason about enhancements or troubleshooting in the future.
</explanation>
